A.explanation: This is only the water gauge pressure $\rho g h$, and it omits the $101 \text{ kPa}$ atmospheric pressure acting on the lake surface.

B.explanation: Pressure increases with depth, so the water pressure cannot be subtracted from atmospheric pressure to give less than $101 \text{ kPa}$.

C.explanation: This adds only about $2 \text{ kPa}$ to atmospheric pressure, much less than the $\rho g h$ increase for $1.50 \text{ m}$ of water.

D.explanation: Total pressure is $p_0 + \rho g h = 101 \text{ kPa} + 14.7 \text{ kPa} \approx 116 \text{ kPa}$.

hints: Notice the pressure at $1.50 \text{ m}$ depth has two parts: the $101 \text{ kPa}$ atmosphere pushing on the lake surface plus the weight of the water above.
Recall the hydrostatic pressure increase is $\Delta p = \rho g h$ with $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and $h = 1.50 \text{ m}$.
Calculate $\rho g h$ in $\text{Pa}$, convert to $\text{kPa}$, then add it to $101 \text{ kPa}$ rather than using it alone.
walkthrough: Identify the givens: depth $h = 1.50 \text{ m}$, water density $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, surface pressure $p_0 = 101 \text{ kPa}$, and $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
State the rule for pressure in a liquid: total pressure $p = p_0 + \rho g h$, where $\rho g h$ is the extra pressure due to the water column.
Calculate the water column term: $\Delta p = \rho g h = 1000 \times 9.81 \times 1.50 = 14715 \text{ Pa}$.
Convert to kilopascals: $14715 \text{ Pa} \approx 14.7 \text{ kPa}$, so this is the gauge pressure at $1.50 \text{ m}$.
Add the atmospheric pressure: $p = 101 \text{ kPa} + 14.7 \text{ kPa} = 115.7 \text{ kPa} \approx 116 \text{ kPa}$.
